headline: Boats worked the Wilmington edge for six hours — three yellowfin and a mahi to show for the fuel burn
subhead: The eddy that's been camped over the canyon for two weeks is still paying rent, but the run has to be worth the diesel.
body_markdown:
The call this week is the same call it's been for two weeks running: troll the edge early, chunk it late if the current lets you sit still. That warm eddy that parked itself over Wilmington Canyon has held its ground longer than most of these things do, and as long as it stays put, the run out of Indian River or Cape May still pencils out. Burn the fuel to get to blue water and a clean temp break, and the bite has been worth the trip more often than not. That's the whole conversation at the dock this week — not whether the fish are there, but whether the eddy survives the next few days of northerly wind and a cooling trend that's been talked about since Labor Day.

We flagged this last week — said the warm water holding would keep pelagic activity steady through the next 72 hours, and that's exactly how it's played out. The filament hasn't broken down. Boats running out to the canyon head, working the color change where the blue water butts up against the greener shelf stuff inshore of the 100-fathom line, have been finding bait balled up tight and tuna sitting under it. That's the setup right now: warm, clean water pushing west against the edge, current ripping hard enough to hold bait in tight seams instead of scattering it across open water.

The troll bite has been the more consistent play through the week. Boats pulling a standard spread — small green machines and cedar plugs down the middle, naked ballyhoo behind spreader bars on the long riggers, a black-and-purple daisy chain teasing a switch bait off the flat line — have been picking off yellowfin in the 20 to 40-pound class along the west wall, right where the canyon starts to drop off hard toward six hundred fathoms. Nobody's filling boxes, but two to four fish for a full morning of trolling has been a fair return, especially with fuel prices what they are. Mahi have been mixed in on the troll too, mostly smaller schoolies in the 5 to 10-pound range holding on scattered weed lines and any bit of floating debris — a welcome bonus fish, not the main event.

White marlin have shown, but it's been a game of patience more than volume. The boats pulling dredge teasers with a naked ballyhoo pitch bait rigged behind have raised fish sporadically along the same temperature seam that's holding the tuna, mostly mid-morning once the sun's had a chance to warm the surface layer. One or two releases for a day's trolling has been the going rate — not a stacked bite, but enough to keep the spread in the water and the crew paying attention.

When the current has laid down enough to hold a solid anchor drift or a controlled drift-chunk, boats working butterfish chunks over the drop-off past the canyon edge have connected with better-grade bluefin, some pushing into the 80 to 150-pound range, along with the occasional bigeye showing up on the deep chunk after dark. That's been a night program mostly — soak butterfish on a long fluorocarbon leader, let it sink out with the chunks, and wait for the current to slow enough that the scent trail actually holds instead of blowing out. Wahoo have come through as incidental fish on the high-speed troll gear when boats have run wire line and a bright skirted lure down deep along the same break — not a targeted program this week, more of a bycatch story, but worth having a rod rigged for it if you're already out there.

The why behind all of this is straightforward. That warm eddy has been sitting over the canyon for better than two weeks now, holding a stable temperature break instead of sliding off to the east like these things sometimes do in a hurry. Bait's been concentrating along that seam, and the tuna and marlin have been following the bait, which is about as simple as this business gets. The risk everyone's watching is a cold-water pinch — a shot of cooler shelf water squeezing in from the north or west that could tighten that break hard against the canyon wall or shove it offshore entirely. If that happens, the smart move is to stop chasing open water and tuck right against the wall itself, working the 100 to 250-fathom contour where the temperature gradient will compress and concentrate whatever's left of the bite.

Looking at the next few days, the pattern should hold if the wind stays out of the south to southwest and doesn't build enough sea to shut down the smaller boats. If a front pushes through with more north in it, expect that eddy to get squeezed and the fish to bunch up tighter along the edge rather than spread out over open water — which actually can concentrate the trolling bite if you're willing to work a smaller piece of real estate instead of running the whole canyon face. Best case, the filament holds through the weekend and this same troll-then-chunk program keeps producing at the same modest but steady clip. Worst case, a cooling trend breaks it up mid-week and the story becomes finding where the fish regroup — likely tight to the canyon wall itself. Either way, this isn't a bite where you run out blind and hope. Check the temp break before you commit the fuel, and if it's not there, save the trip for a better window.
